25967: Luke 7:12 says he was 'the only son of his mother, and she was a widow'. Luke 7:13 says the Lord had compassion on her. Luke 7:15 says Jesus gave him to his mother, words that echo Elijah raising the widow of Zarephath's son (1 Kgs 17:23).
25969: Most commentators note the parallel with Elijah (1 Kgs 17:17-24) and Elisha, who raised the Shunammite's son at nearby Shunem (2 Kgs 4:32-37). The crowd's cry that a great prophet has arisen shows they understood the link.
25970: The story is often used to show Jesus' compassion for the grieving and for vulnerable women, since he acts before anyone asks.
25971: The mother: numb with grief, then overwhelmed. The son: confused, then joyfully talking.
25973: The text does not give her name; 'Syrophoenician' means a Phoenician from the province of Syria
25977: Gentile mother who sought healing for her daughter
25979: 'Even the dogs eat the children's crumbs'
25980: In the region of Tyre she begs Jesus to free her daughter from an unclean spirit. Jesus answers that the children (Israel) must be fed first and it is not right to throw their bread to the dogs. She replies that even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs. Jesus praises her answer (in Matthew, her great faith) and her daughter is healed at a distance.
25981: This unnamed Gentile woman came to Jesus near Tyre to ask him to heal her daughter. Jesus' first reply sounds harsh, using a common image of Gentiles as 'dogs'. She did not argue against him but took his own words and turned them into a request, and he granted it. She is the only person in the Gospels who wins an exchange of words with Jesus.
25982: Mark 7:26 calls her 'a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth'. Matthew 15:22 calls her 'a Canaanite woman' and has her address Jesus as 'Son of David'. Matthew 15:24 has Jesus say he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel. Matthew 15:28 has Jesus say 'great is your faith'.
25984: Many traditional interpreters say Jesus was testing and drawing out her faith, knowing he would help her.
25986: Others stress that Jesus' mission was to Israel first, then to the nations (compare Rom 1:16), and that her story anticipates the Gentile mission.
25988: Some modern interpreters think Jesus, being truly human, was genuinely moved by her reply to widen the scope of his ministry; others object that this conflicts with his knowledge and purpose elsewhere.
25989: The Pseudo-Clementine writings name her Justa and her daughter Bernice.
25991: Desperate but clever, humble but unwilling to take no for an answer.
25994: 'Let him who is without sin cast the first stone'
25995: In the Temple courts, scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery and ask whether she should be stoned as the Law of Moses commands, hoping to trap Jesus. He writes on the ground, then says that whoever is without sin should throw the first stone. They leave one by one. Jesus tells her, 'Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.'
25996: This unnamed woman was brought to Jesus in the Temple as a test case: should she be stoned for adultery? Jesus turned the question back on her accusers, who left, and then sent her away uncondemned but told to stop sinning. The story is one of the best loved in the Gospels, but it is also the best known textual puzzle in the New Testament: it is missing from the earliest and most important manuscripts of John.
25997: John 8:4-5 records the charge and the appeal to the Law (compare Lev 20:10; Deut 22:22). John 8:6 says they were testing him. John 8:7 records his saying about the first stone. John 8:11 records his words to her. The man involved is not mentioned.
25998: The passage (John 7:53-8:11) does not appear in the earliest Greek manuscripts of John (including Papyrus 66, Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus). It first appears in a Greek manuscript in Codex Bezae (about AD 400), and in other manuscripts it is placed elsewhere, for example after Luke 21:38 or after John 7:36. Modern Bibles usually print it with a note or in brackets.
25999: Not original to John, but authentic tradition (scholarly consensus on the first part)
26000: Most textual scholars agree it was not part of John as first written. Many still think it preserves a genuine early story about Jesus, which circulated separately before being added to John.
26002: A minority argue it was originally in John and was removed early, perhaps because some feared it seemed too lenient on adultery.
26004: Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches treat it as Scripture or as a reliable account, while being open about its textual history.
26005: Terrified and silent at first, then stunned to be spoken to with dignity.
26007: The text does not give his name; a centurion commanded about 80 to 100 soldiers
26008: Gentile soldier, probably in Herod Antipas's service
26009: Gentile officer whose servant Jesus healed
26010: Faith that Jesus' word is enough
26013: His valued servant is paralysed and near death. He asks Jesus for help but says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof: as a man under authority who gives orders, he knows Jesus need only speak. Jesus marvels and says he has not found such faith in Israel. The servant is healed at that hour.
26014: This unnamed centurion was a Gentile officer stationed at Capernaum, probably serving Herod Antipas rather than the Roman army directly. He loved the Jewish people and had built their synagogue. When his servant was dying, he trusted that Jesus could heal from a distance by a word, and Jesus said he had not found such faith anywhere in Israel. His words 'Lord, I am not worthy' are still repeated in many communion liturgies.
26015: Matthew 8:5-6 has the centurion come to Jesus himself. Luke 7:3-6 has him send Jewish elders and then friends, who say he loves the nation and built the synagogue. Matthew 8:11-12 adds Jesus' saying that many will come from east and west to sit with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
26016: Ancient custom treated a messenger as the sender, so Matthew may simply shorten the story by having the centurion speak directly, while Luke gives the fuller account.
26018: Some scholars think John's story of a royal official at Capernaum whose son is healed from Cana (John 4:46-54) is a version of the same event; others think it is a separate miracle.
26020: Catholic, Anglican and other liturgies adapt his words before communion: 'Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word.'
26021: Disciplined, respectful and economical with words, a commander who knows the power of a single order.
26025: member of the first Jerusalem church
26026: Lies about the gift and dies
26027: Ananias sold a piece of land, kept back part of the money with his wife's knowledge, and laid the rest at the apostles' feet as if it were the whole. Peter told him he had lied not to people but to God, and Ananias fell down and died.
26028: Ananias was a member of the earliest church in Jerusalem. He and his wife Sapphira sold property and pretended to give the full price to the apostles while secretly keeping part of it. When Peter exposed the lie, Ananias fell dead, and great fear came over the church.
26029: Acts stresses that the land and the money were his to keep (Acts 5:4). The sin was not keeping money but pretending, and Peter calls it lying to the Holy Spirit and to God (Acts 5:3-4). The story directly follows the generous example of Barnabas (Acts 4:36-37).
26031: A warning that the church's holiness is real and that hypocrisy before God is serious, set at the very start of the church as Achan's sin was at the start of Israel's life in the land (Josh 7).
26033: Some scholars read the episode as a literary echo of the Achan story meant to teach a lesson; others note its harshness has troubled readers since antiquity and ask whether Peter pronounced judgement or simply revealed it.
26034: Eager to look generous and quick to rehearse a story; speaks smoothly but grows uneasy when asked direct questions.
26038: About three hours after her husband's death, Sapphira came in not knowing what had happened. Peter asked whether the land had sold for the stated price; she said yes, and she too fell dead.
26039: Sapphira was the wife of Ananias and shared in his plan to hold back part of the money from a land sale while claiming to give all of it. Questioned separately by Peter, she repeated the lie and died at once. Acts says that great fear came on the whole church.
26040: Acts says she knew about the plan (Acts 5:2) and that Peter gave her a chance to tell the truth by asking the price directly (Acts 5:8). Peter calls their agreement a testing of the Spirit of the Lord (Acts 5:9).
26041: Her story shows that each person is answerable to God for their own choices, even within a marriage.
26043: Some readers note that she is judged as a full moral agent, not as an extension of her husband; others find the episode's severity difficult and stress that Acts presents it as unique, not a pattern for church discipline.
26044: Composed and careful, answering exactly what is asked and no more.
26050: Called in a vision to visit Saul
26051: The Lord told Ananias in a vision to go to Straight Street and lay hands on Saul of Tarsus. Ananias objected that Saul had come to arrest believers, but the Lord said Saul was a chosen instrument to carry his name to Gentiles, kings and Israel.
26052: Restores Saul's sight and baptizes him
26053: Ananias greeted him as 'Brother Saul', laid hands on him, and something like scales fell from Saul's eyes. Saul was baptized and was filled with the Holy Spirit.
26055: Years later Paul described Ananias to a Jerusalem crowd as a devout man who kept the Law and was well spoken of by all the Jews in Damascus.
26056: Ananias was a believer in Damascus whom God sent to the newly blinded Saul of Tarsus, the very man who had come to arrest Christians. Despite his fear, he went, called Saul 'brother', restored his sight and baptized him. Paul later described him as a devout, Law-keeping Jew respected by the whole Jewish community of Damascus.
26057: Acts records his honest objection (Acts 9:13-14) and his obedience. In Paul's own retelling, Ananias tells Saul he has been chosen to know God's will and to be a witness to all people (Acts 22:14-15).
26058: A model of costly obedience and welcome: the first Christian to treat the persecutor as family.
26060: His presence shows that a community of Jesus-followers existed in Damascus very early, before Paul's mission; scholars debate how the three conversion accounts in Acts (Acts 9, Acts 22, Acts 26) relate to one another.
26061: Later tradition counts him among the seventy disciples, makes him bishop of Damascus, and says he died as a martyr. These stories are late and not historically secure.
26062: Eastern church calendars and later lists of the Seventy (e.g. attributed to Dorotheus of Tyre); late, needs verification
26063: Plain-spoken and honest about his fears, but warm once he acts; he says 'brother' and means it.
26070: When Paul began his defense before the council, Ananias ordered those near him to strike him on the mouth. Paul called him a 'whitewashed wall', then apologised when told he was the high priest, quoting the command not to speak evil of a ruler (Exod 22:28).
26072: Five days later Ananias went down to Caesarea with elders and the lawyer Tertullus to press charges against Paul before the governor Felix.
26073: Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest in Jerusalem from about AD 47 to 59. Acts shows him ordering Paul to be struck during a council hearing and then travelling to Caesarea to accuse him before the governor Felix. The Jewish historian Josephus describes him as wealthy and grasping, and reports that he was killed by Jewish rebels at the start of the war with Rome in AD 66.
26074: Acts records only his command to strike Paul, Paul's sharp reply and apology, and his role as accuser at Caesarea (Acts 23:2-5; Acts 24:1).
26076: Readers differ on Acts 23:5: some think Paul genuinely did not recognise him (poor eyesight, or an informal meeting); others read it as irony, meaning a man acting that way did not look like a high priest.
26077: High priests in this period were appointed and removed by Roman or Herodian rulers. Josephus says Ananias was sent to Rome for trial around AD 52 and returned, kept influence after leaving office, and that his servants seized tithes owed to ordinary priests.
26078: Josephus describes his appointment and later his greed and influence.
26080: Josephus reports that he was killed by rebels early in the Jewish revolt (AD 66).
26082: Imperious and short-tempered, used to giving orders in a council chamber and expecting them obeyed.
26089: Simon practised magic and claimed to be someone great; people of every rank called him 'the power of God that is called Great'.
26091: When Philip preached and worked signs, Simon himself believed, was baptized and stayed close to Philip, amazed at the miracles.
26092: Tries to buy the power to give the Spirit
26093: Seeing that the Spirit was given when Peter and John laid on hands, Simon offered money for the same power. Peter rebuked him sharply, told him to repent, and Simon asked them to pray for him.
26094: Simon was a well-known magician in Samaria who was baptized after hearing Philip preach. When he saw the apostles Peter and John lay hands on people to receive the Holy Spirit, he offered them money for the same ability, and Peter rebuked him. His name gave us the word 'simony', the buying or selling of church offices. Early Christian writers later made him the father of heresy, though how much of that picture is history is uncertain.
26095: Acts says Simon 'believed' and was baptized (Acts 8:13), yet Peter says his heart is not right before God and that he is in the 'gall of bitterness' (Acts 8:21-23). The story ends with Simon asking for prayer, and Acts does not say what became of him (Acts 8:24).
26097: Some read Simon as a false convert whose belief was only fascination with power; others see a genuine but immature believer who was rebuked and responded. The text leaves his final state open.
26099: Second-century writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus treat him as the founder of a Gnostic sect (Gnostics claimed secret knowledge brought salvation) and as the source of later heresies.
26101: Most think the later legends grew far beyond the Acts account; whether the historical Simon really founded a movement is debated.
26102: Justin Martyr says Simon went to Rome under Claudius and was honoured as a god there with a statue. Justin probably misread an inscription to the Sabine god Semo Sancus found in 1574.
26104: Irenaeus presents Simon as the source of all heresies and describes his companion Helen.
26106: Later legends describe a contest of miracles between Simon and Peter in Rome, ending with Simon falling while trying to fly.
26108: Showman's patter, confident and grand, quick to bargain; becomes anxious and pleading when crossed by real authority.
26111: servant girl in the house of Mary, mother of John Mark
26113: Leaves Peter standing at the gate
26114: After Peter's escape from prison, he knocked at the gate where the church was praying. Rhoda recognised his voice and was so glad that she ran in to tell the others without opening the gate. They told her she was out of her mind, but Peter kept knocking.
26115: Rhoda was a servant girl in the Jerusalem house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where believers met to pray. When Peter, freed from prison by an angel, knocked at the gate, she recognised his voice and in her joy ran to announce him without letting him in. Her scene is one of the warmest and most humorous in Acts.
26116: The praying believers dismissed her report and said 'It is his angel', but she kept insisting until they opened the gate (Acts 12:15-16).
26117: Excited and breathless, insistent when no one believes her.
26120: young man in the church at Troas
26121: Falls from a window and is restored
26122: During Paul's long talk on the first day of the week, Eutychus sat in a third-storey window, fell asleep and fell to his death. Paul went down, embraced him and said his life was in him. The church was greatly comforted to take the young man home alive.
26123: Eutychus was a young man in Troas who dozed off in a window while Paul preached late into the night, fell three storeys and was picked up dead. Paul went down, took him in his arms, and he was restored to life. The meeting then went on until dawn.
26124: Luke, who appears to be present (the 'we' passages), says he was 'taken up dead' (Acts 20:9). Paul's words 'his life is in him' (Acts 20:10) have led a minority to think he was only unconscious, though most readers take Luke to describe a raising from the dead like those of Elijah and Elisha (1 Kgs 17:21; 2 Kgs 4:34).
26125: Shy and a little sheepish, a teenager who knows everyone remembers him as the one who fell asleep.
26127: Later date for the first missionary journey
26132: Luke calls him an intelligent man who sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God.
26133: Believes after Elymas is struck blind
26134: When the magician Elymas opposed them, Paul declared that he would be blind for a time, and he was. The proconsul believed, astonished at the teaching about the Lord.
26135: Sergius Paulus was the Roman proconsul, or governor, of Cyprus when Barnabas and Paul visited the island on their first missionary journey. He invited them to speak, watched Paul confront the court magician Elymas, and believed. From this point Acts begins calling Saul by his Roman name, Paul.
26136: Luke uses the correct title 'proconsul' for the governor of Cyprus, which was a senatorial province at the time (Acts 13:7). He says the proconsul 'believed' (Acts 13:12) without describing baptism.
26138: Many read Acts 13:12 as a real conversion; others think Luke describes impressed interest rather than full commitment, since no baptism is mentioned.
26140: Inscriptions name members of a senatorial family, the Sergii Paulli, including a Lucius Sergius Paullus who served on a Tiber river board in Rome under Claudius, and family estates near Pisidian Antioch. Some scholars link these to the proconsul (and suggest it explains why Paul went next to Pisidian Antioch); others think the identification is unproven.
26141: Measured, curious and courteous, a cultured Roman official who asks good questions.
26143: Probably 'sorcerer' or 'wise man'; the meaning of Elymas is debated
26146: magician and false prophet at the proconsul's court
26147: Opposes Paul and is struck blind
26148: Elymas tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Paul, filled with the Spirit, called him a son of the devil and said the Lord's hand would make him blind for a time. Mist and darkness fell on him and he groped for someone to lead him.
26149: Elymas, also called Bar-Jesus, was a Jewish magician and self-styled prophet attached to the court of Sergius Paulus, the governor of Cyprus. When he tried to stop the governor from believing Paul and Barnabas, Paul declared that he would be blind for a while, and it happened at once. The governor believed.
26150: Acts calls him a 'false prophet' (Acts 13:6) and says the blindness would last 'for a time' (Acts 13:11), which some see as leaving room for repentance.
26151: Clever and sly, used to flattering powerful patrons and undermining rivals.
26153: Belonging to Demeter (the Greek harvest goddess)
26157: leader of the riot at Ephesus
26160: Demetrius, who made silver shrines of Artemis, gathered his fellow workers and warned that Paul's teaching that 'gods made with hands are not gods' threatened both their trade and the honour of the great goddess Artemis.
26162: The crowd shouted 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians' for about two hours in the theatre, dragging in Paul's companions Gaius and Aristarchus, until the town clerk calmed them and told Demetrius to use the courts.
26163: Demetrius was a silversmith in Ephesus who made small silver shrines of the goddess Artemis, whose huge temple made the city famous. As Paul's preaching drew people away from idols, Demetrius rallied the craftsmen with a speech that mixed business worries with religious pride. The result was a city-wide riot in the theatre, calmed only by the town clerk.
26164: Acts lets Demetrius state his own motives honestly: lost income and the goddess's prestige (Acts 19:25-27). The town clerk points out that Paul's companions had neither robbed temples nor blasphemed the goddess (Acts 19:37).
26166: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Small figurines and souvenir shrines of Artemis are well attested, though silver 'shrines' themselves have not been found; some suggest they were melted down.
26167: Often read as a picture of how the gospel can threaten economic interests, and how religion and money can be bound together.
26168: A persuasive trade-guild orator who talks about wages and civic pride in the same breath.
26172: Some place his death slightly later, after the Pisonian conspiracy fallout
26175: Throws out the case against Paul
26176: Jewish leaders in Corinth brought Paul before Gallio's judgement seat, accusing him of teaching worship contrary to the law. Gallio ruled that this was a dispute about words, names and their own law, not a crime, and drove them from the tribunal.
26178: The crowd then beat Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, in front of the tribunal, and Gallio paid no attention.
26179: Gallio was the Roman proconsul, or governor, of the province of Achaia (southern Greece), based in Corinth. When Jewish leaders accused Paul before him, he refused to judge what he saw as an internal religious quarrel. Gallio is one of the most important anchors for New Testament dating: an inscription found at Delphi places his term of office around AD 51–52, which lets scholars date Paul's stay in Corinth and, from there, much of his career.
26180: Acts uses the correct title, proconsul, for a governor of Achaia (Acts 18:12). Gallio's ruling treats the Christian movement as a matter within Judaism, not a new illegal religion (Acts 18:14-15).
26182: Most scholars date Paul's arrival in Corinth to about AD 50 and his hearing before Gallio to about AD 51 or 52, using the Delphi inscription. Debate continues over whether Gallio arrived in summer 51 or 52, and whether Paul's hearing came early or late in Gallio's term.
26184: Many think Luke includes the ruling to show that Roman officials found nothing criminal in Christianity; others caution that Gallio's indifference to the beating of Sosthenes is hardly flattering.
26185: Gallio was the older brother of the philosopher Seneca, Nero's tutor, and took the name Gallio after being adopted by the orator Lucius Junius Gallio. Seneca mentions that Gallio left Achaia because of a fever. Like Seneca, he fell from favour after the plot against Nero in AD 65.
